title: Design a knowledge base and memory layer for government AI agents
evidence: This mirrors a product GovTech's Giant Robots Labs lists publicly (GovBrain, "an agent memory and knowledge base for managing government knowledge"); it is practice, not a reported interview question.
prompt:
"Officers across agencies are starting to use AI agents. Design the knowledge base and memory those agents use: they should answer from agency documents with citations, and remember things about the officer between sessions."

The interviewer will push on who can see what, and on how you would know it works.

clarify.q: Which sources, and how many documents?
clarify.a: Shared drives, wikis and intranet sites from several agencies. Assume about 10 million documents.

clarify.q: Who uses it, and how much?
clarify.a: Up to 150k officers through agents; assume 30% active on a given day, about 10 questions each.

clarify.q: What is the highest classification allowed?
clarify.a: RESTRICTED / SENSITIVE NORMAL. Anything higher must not enter the system.
Yes. Each source has its own access lists, and an officer must only ever see what they could open at the source.
Preferences and facts about the officer, and summaries of past tasks. Officers must be able to see and delete them.

clarify.q: How fast must changes and deletions show up?
clarify.a: Edits within a few minutes. A deleted document must stop appearing in answers almost immediately.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: List functional and non-functional requirements. Which one shapes the design most?
steps.model:
• Functional: ingest and sync many sources; answer with citations or say "not found"; agents read and write memories via a tool API (MCP); deletes propagate; users see and delete their memories.
  • Non-functional: per-user access enforced at retrieval; retrieval p95 < 300 ms, answer p95 < 4 s; edits searchable in ~2 min; data within the RESTRICTED / SENSITIVE NORMAL ceiling and in-region; every access audited.

Say: "Access control shapes everything. I'll enforce it in the retrieval query, never in the prompt."

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Size the index, the query rate and the embedding cost.
steps.model:
• 10M docs × 20 chunks = 200M chunks; 1,024-dim float32 = ~820 GB, ~205 GB with int8.
  • 150k × 30% × 10 = 450k questions/day, ~5/s average, ~150 searches/s at peak with agents searching 3 times per task.
  • Backfill: 200M × 400 tokens = 80B tokens, about $1,600 at $0.02 per 1M tokens. Daily churn is ~200k chunks.

Conclusion: embedding is cheap; the index size and the reranker and LLM GPUs are the real costs.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: Define the tool API agents call and the main tables.
steps.model:
• search_knowledge (POST /v1/search), answer, remember, recall, forget. ACL comes from the caller's delegated token, never the request body.
  • documents: doc_id, source_uri, owner_agency, classification, acl_groups[], version, content_hash, deleted_at.
  • chunks: chunk_id, doc_id, version, text, heading_path, embedding, classification, acl_groups[].
  • memories: memory_id, owner_user_id, type (preference | fact | episode), content, embedding, source_refs[], expires_at, superseded_by.
  • Session buffer in Redis with a 24 h TTL.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the components. Walk one ingest and one question end to end.
steps.model:
Ingest: connectors (webhooks + nightly listing) → queue keyed by (doc_id, version) → workers parse, chunk ~400 tokens with heading paths, stamp ACL and classification, embed changed chunks only → Postgres (source of truth) and a hybrid index (BM25 + vectors + ACL fields).

Question: agent → MCP gateway (authn, audit) → resolve user groups → hybrid search with the ACL filter inside the query, ~50 candidates each, fused with RRF → cross-encoder rerank to 8 → LLM answers only from those 8 and cites them, or abstains. User memories are recalled in the same step, filtered by owner.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on access control and deletion, then on how you evaluate quality.
steps.model:
Access: pre-filter in the query, not post-filter (post-filtering can return nothing and leaks counts). The agent acts with the officer's token. ACL changes re-stamp chunk metadata without re-embedding; group caches live minutes.

Deletion: tombstone first so answers stop in seconds, then delete chunks, vectors, caches and memories whose source_refs point at the doc; hard-delete rows after a retention window. Public agencies follow the Public Sector (Governance) Act and government data rules rather than the PDPA, but the duty is the same: every derived copy must go.

Evals: a golden set of ~400 questions with acting users and expected doc ids. Measure recall@8, groundedness, abstention and a zero-tolerance leak test on every change to chunking, models, prompts or ranking; block releases on regression.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.model:
• Prompt injection via documents: treat retrieved text as data, flag instruction-like text at ingest, no side-effecting tools in the answer step, confirmation for agent actions.
  • Latency: reranker and LLM dominate; rerank only 50, stream, cache per (query, ACL group set).
  • Backfill: separate low-priority queue, build a new index behind an alias.
  • Memory quality: typed writes, de-duplication, expiry and a user-visible list, versus free-form notes that drift.

rubric: Enforces per-user access inside the retrieval query and says the prompt is not a control.
Stamps ACL, owner agency and classification on every chunk at ingest.
Uses hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vectors) and explains what each catches, with a reranker on a small candidate set.
Answers with citations to retrieved chunks and abstains when the answer is not found.
Distinguishes short-term, long-term and episodic memory, scoped per user and visible to the user.
Handles deletion with a tombstone and propagates it to vectors, caches and derived memories.
Defines evals (golden set, recall@k, groundedness, leak test) run on every change.
Names prompt injection through ingested documents and a concrete defence.
Respects the classification ceiling (e.g. RESTRICTED / SENSITIVE NORMAL) and keeps data in-region.
